name: TypeOut
tagline: Hold a hotkey, talk, and get cleaned-up text typed into whatever app you are in.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The transcription itself is a solved commodity: Whisper-class models run locally on a modern laptop, and a hotkey-to-clipboard-to-paste loop is a couple hundred lines. What you are actually paying for is the boring part, a background process that never crashes, cold-start latency under a second, correct behavior across every text field in every app, and an LLM cleanup pass that removes filler words without inventing sentences. An agent gets you a working personal version in a sitting, but the first week of living with it will surface permission dialogs, focus-stealing bugs, and dictation into Slack that drops the first syllable. If you dictate occasionally, build it. If dictation is how you write all day, the polish tax is real.
coreLoopDIY: A menu bar daemon that records while a global hotkey is held, transcribes locally with Whisper, optionally cleans the text with an LLM, and pastes it into the focused app.
requirements: macOS with Apple Silicon for usable local Whisper speed
Accessibility and Microphone permissions granted to the terminal or packaged app
Optional OpenAI or Anthropic key in .env if you want the cleanup pass
Roughly 1 to 3 GB of disk for the model weights
whatYouLose: Sub-second cold start and a model that stays warm without eating RAM
Reliable text insertion in apps with odd input handling, Electron and remote desktops especially
Custom vocabulary, names, and jargon that stick across sessions
iOS or cross-device use, your build is one machine only
Someone else fixing it when a macOS update breaks the Accessibility API
moatNotes: The moat is latency and never-fails insertion, not the speech model. Everyone in this category uses roughly the same weights.
whyPeopleStillPay: Dictation is a tool you use mid-thought, which means any friction kills it outright. A build that works 95 percent of the time is worse than useless because you stop trusting it and go back to typing. Paid dictation apps are mostly a bet that someone else will keep the hotkey responsive, the model warm, and the paste reliable across OS updates, and for people who dictate thousands of words a day that bet is cheap.
notes: Build this one if only to learn how thin the speech-to-text layer actually is.
prompt:
Build a local, system-wide push-to-talk dictation tool for macOS. No accounts, no cloud transcription, no telemetry.

Stack, use exactly this:
- Python 3.11 managed with uv, single project in the current folder
- rumps for the menu bar app
- sounddevice + numpy to capture 16 kHz mono audio
- faster-whisper for local transcription, default model "small.en", configurable in config.toml
- pynput for the global hotkey
- pyobjc to read the frontmost app and to paste via a synthetic Cmd+V

Behavior:
- Hold Right Option to record. Release to stop. Show a recording state in the menu bar icon.
- On release, transcribe the buffer locally. Target under 1.5 seconds for a 10 second clip.
- Optional cleanup pass: if OPENAI_API_KEY is in .env, send the raw transcript to gpt-4o-mini with a strict prompt that only removes filler words and fixes punctuation and casing, and never adds content. If no key, skip it and use the raw transcript.
- Put the final text on the clipboard, restore the previous clipboard contents after pasting, and send Cmd+V to the frontmost app.
- Keep the Whisper model loaded in memory between dictations so there is no cold start.
- Keep a plain text log of the last 50 transcripts in ~/.typeout/history.txt so I can recover a lost dictation.

Config in config.toml: model size, hotkey, cleanup on/off, custom vocabulary list that gets passed to Whisper as an initial prompt.

Out of scope: iOS, any sync, any GUI beyond the menu bar, speaker diarization, real-time streaming transcription.

Write a README that spells out the Accessibility and Microphone permission steps, because the app silently does nothing without them. Include a smoke test script that records 3 seconds from the mic and prints the transcript so I can verify the pipeline before wiring up the hotkey.
